criteria.rationale: The story materially foregrounds the sciences (geology, mineralogy, anthropology, linguistics), and frames its horror explicitly around the correlation of dissociated scientific knowledge; the idol's stone is analyzed as matching no known rock, and the Old Ones' non-material composition and telepathy function as speculative-science content.

No engineered device, technique, or invention materially affects the setting, problem, or outcome. The idols and ships are ordinary or ancient artifacts, not inventions driving the action; the carven idols are cult objects rather than functional technology.

The narrative centrally invokes a hugely remote past (the Great Old Ones who ruled eons before humanity, R'lyeh built in measureless eons, Cthulhu loose after vigintillions of years) and situates present events against these vast temporal displacements.

From the premise of the entombed Old Ones awaiting the stars' alignment, the story extrapolates consequences: Castro's prophecy of humanity degenerating into lawless revelry when the stars are right, and the narrator's extrapolation that fully correlating knowledge will unleash catastrophic revelation.

Systematic inquiry materially drives understanding: Angell instituted a far-flung body of dream inquiries with dated reports, questioned Wilcox with scientific minuteness, and Legrasse and Webb conducted an exhaustive comparison of ritual chants; geologists measured and evaluated the stone. The whole plot advances by piecing together evidence.

Cosmic visitors from the stars (the Great Old Ones who came from the sky) and a substantially nonordinary environment (R'lyeh with its non-Euclidean, impossibly distorted geometry, on an uncharted island) are central to the story.

The awakening and emergence of Cthulhu represents an impending cosmic catastrophe of global scale; the prophesied return would see the earth flame with a holocaust of ecstasy and the world screaming with fright. It is averted only by chance sinking, remaining causally central and impending.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story develops a coherent, systematic, immanent account: the Old Ones are presented not as supernatural gods but as material (though non-earthly matter) beings governed by stellar cycles, transmitted-thought communication, and a corroborating body of investigative evidence (cross-cult ritual identity, correlated dream reports, geological analysis). The framing of scientific correlation of dissociated knowledge and immanent cosmic law satisfies cognitive validation without requiring present-day buildability.

candidates.description: The Great Old Ones, cosmic entities epitomized by Cthulhu, who came from the stars in a hugely remote prehuman epoch, lie in death-like dormancy in the sunken stone city of R'lyeh, communicate through transmitted thought and dream-molding, and await a cyclical stellar alignment to rise and reclaim the earth. This candidate constitutes the totalizing cosmology of the story in which humanity is a transient, insignificant incident.

estrangement.rationale: The reader is estranged by the contrast between the placid island of human ignorance and the hidden totality of a hostile cosmos, dramatized through investigators' confidence-shattering discoveries and the madness/death of witnesses.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The entire narrative logic—the dreams, the cult raids, the cross-continental correlations, the sea voyage, the narrator's dread—derives from and converges on the reality of Cthulhu and the Old Ones. It governs the overriding narrative consequences and is the organizing novum, not an incidental device.

novelty.rationale: The existence of star-born entities predating humanity, dormant beneath earth and sea, awaiting cyclical resurrection, is a totalizing difference from the empirical norm that reframes the entire status of humanity and the cosmos. It alters a crucial aspect of the story universe rather than presenting an isolated oddity.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story appeals to the systematic, non-supernatural concept of non-Euclidean geometry and 'dimensions apart from ours,' corroborated independently by both the sculptor's dream and an unlettered seaman's observation, giving it an immanent cognitive logic.

candidates.description: R'lyeh, the sunken corpse-city built in measureless eons, whose non-Euclidean geometry distorts space, light, and perspective—angles that are acute yet behave as obtuse, surfaces where convexity and concavity invert on second glance.

estrangement.rationale: The reader confronts space itself behaving wrongly—ordinary geometry contrasted with impossible angles—producing estrangement through the collapse of trusted physical intuitions.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: R'lyeh is a powerful setting and atmospheric device, but its narrative function is subordinate to and derivative of the Cthulhu/Old Ones cosmology; it is the tomb and stage rather than the governing narrative logic in itself. Its centrality is significant but not independently determinative of the whole story.

novelty.rationale: A locus where the fundamental rules of geometry and matter are altered represents a world-altering difference from the empirical norm.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The idol is examined through systematic geological and philological inquiry that coherently concludes it is of unearthly material and cross-culturally identical form, providing an immanent, scientifically framed account.

candidates.description: The carven idol of Cthulhu, made of soapy greenish-black stone with golden flecks that resembles no known rock in geology or mineralogy, brought from the stars and reproduced identically by cults separated by thousands of miles.

estrangement.rationale: The reader is estranged by expert scientists uniformly baffled by a stone that the world holds no parallel to, contrasting ordinary mineralogy with an object from beyond earth.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The idol functions as an investigative clue and piece of corroborating evidence pointing to the Old Ones novum; it is an incidental artifact that does not determine the overriding narrative logic. It lacks story-level governance of consequences on its own.

novelty.rationale: A material unknown to earthly science and of extraterrestrial origin is a genuine difference from the empirical norm.

records.paraphrase: Legrasse and Webb compare ritual chants from geographically distant cults and find them nearly identical.
records.quote: There then followed an exhaustive comparison of details, and a moment of really awed silence when both detective and scientist agreed on the virtual identity of the phrase common to two hellish rituals so many worlds of distance apart.

records.paraphrase: The crew lands on an island that reportedly does not exist on any chart of that ocean region.
records.quote: The next day, it appears, they raised and landed on a small island, although none is known to exist in that part of the ocean

records.paraphrase: Scientific experts examine the idol's stone and conclude it matches no known rock on earth.
records.quote: Geologists, the curator told me, had found it a monstrous puzzle; for they vowed that the world held no rock like it.

records.paraphrase: Castro predicts a future when humans become like the Old Ones, abandoning morals and descending into violent revelry.
records.quote: The time would be easy to know, for then mankind would have become as the Great Old Ones; free and wild and beyond good and evil, with laws and morals thrown aside and all men shouting and killing and reveling in joy.

records.paraphrase: A sailor, Briden, goes insane after seeing Cthulhu and laughs until he dies.
records.quote: Briden looked back and went mad, laughing shrilly as he kept on laughing at intervals till death found him one night in the cabin

records.paraphrase: The gigantic creature Cthulhu emerges from the opened door of the city.
records.quote: It lumbered slobberingly into sight and gropingly squeezed Its gelatinous green immensity through the black doorway into the tainted outside air of that poison city of madness.

records.paraphrase: The narrator frames the dangers of correlating scientific knowledge, warning that piecing together dissociated data will reveal terrifying realities.
records.quote: We live on a placid island of ignorance in the midst of black seas of infinity, and it was not meant that we should voyage far. The sciences, each straining in its own direction, have hitherto harmed us little; but some day the piecing together of dissociated knowledge will open up such terrifying vistas of reality

records.paraphrase: The narrator describes his permanent dread and expectation of early death after learning the truth.
records.quote: I have looked upon all that the universe has to hold of horror, and even the skies of spring and the flowers of summer must ever afterward be poison to me. But I do not think my life will be long.

records.paraphrase: The professor systematically collected dream reports and dates from many people to compile a data digest.
records.quote: My uncle, it seems, had quickly instituted a prodigiously far-flung body of inquiries amongst nearly all the friends whom he could question without impertinence, asking for nightly reports of their dreams, and the dates of any notable visions for some time past.

records.paraphrase: After immense spans of time, Cthulhu is freed and active.
records.quote: After vigintillions of years great Cthulhu was loose again, and ravening for delight.

records.paraphrase: The statuette's material is described as unrecognizable to known geology or mineralogy.
records.quote: the soapy, greenish-black stone with its golden or iridescent flecks and striations resembled nothing familiar to geology or mineralogy

records.paraphrase: The cult explains that ancient beings, the Great Old Ones, came from the sky before humanity and now lie hidden inside earth and sea.
records.quote: They worshiped, so they said, the Great Old Ones who lived ages before there were any men, and who came to the young world out of the sky. Those Old Ones were gone now, inside the earth and under the sea

records.paraphrase: Wilcox dreams of an immense alien city of massive blocks and monoliths covered in green ooze.
records.quote: he had had an unprecedented dream of great Cyclopean cities of Titan blocks and sky-flung monoliths, all dripping with green ooze and sinister with latent horror

records.paraphrase: At R'lyeh the visual environment and angles behave in distorted, impossible ways.
records.quote: The very sun of heaven seemed distorted when viewed through the polarizing miasma welling out from this sea-soaked perversion, and twisted menace and suspense lurked leeringly in those crazily elusive angles of carven rock where a second glance showed concavity after the first showed convexity.

records.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts human mental limitation with the hidden totality of reality, treating ignorance as protective.
records.quote: the most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents

records.paraphrase: Professor Angell interrogates Wilcox methodically and studies the bas-relief with intense analytical attention.
records.quote: He questioned the sculptor with scientific minuteness; and studied with almost frantic intensity the bas-relief on which the youth had found himself working

records.paraphrase: The story contrasts ordinary geometry with the non-Euclidean, alien spatial properties experienced both in dreams and in reality.
records.quote: the geometry of the dream-place he saw was abnormal, non-Euclidean, and loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours. Now an unlettered seaman felt the same thing whilst gazing at the terrible reality.

records.paraphrase: The Old Ones communicate via transmitted thought and remain aware of the universe from their tombs.
records.quote: They knew all that was occurring in the universe, for Their mode of speech was transmitted thought. Even now They talked in Their tombs.
